title: Single-exponential Directed Feedback Vertex Set
formal: Do there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm and constants \(A,c>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\), which decide Directed Feedback Vertex Set on every \(n\)-vertex directed graph and deletion budget \(0\le k\le n\) within \(A\,2^{ck}(n+1)^d\) bit-computation steps? The answer must be YES exactly when deleting at most \(k\) vertices makes the graph acyclic. The exponential dependence is solely on the solution-size budget, and the polynomial exponent is independent of \(k\).
why: Deleting a small number of vertices to destroy every directed cycle is a basic model of repairing cyclic dependencies. Fixed-parameter algorithms make small deletion budgets tractable in principle, but the known factorial dependence is much larger than a fixed exponential base. The target asks whether directed cycle structure inherently causes that additional parameter cost.
status_note: The checked 2025 primary papers retain the general single-exponential parameter question or the stronger unresolved subfactorial improvement. The SOSA 2025 bound retains k! and does not settle the target. Bounded subsequent-result checks through 2026-09-16 verified no general resolution; this is not an exhaustive certification of current openness.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-16; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: As reviewed in the checked survey and later primary papers, Chen, Liu, Lu, O’Sullivan and Razgon establish fixed-parameter tractability with \(2^{O(k\log k)}n^{O(1)}\) running time.
The checked survey v2 states the single-exponential general vertex/arc question and the separate planar vertex question in Open Problem 3.3.
Xiong and Xiao’s SOSA paper gives \(O(k!\,2^{o(k)}(n+m))\) time. Its checked October 2024 preprint states this in Theorem 3 and still describes single-exponential dependence as open.
Dirks, Gerhard, Grobler, Mouawad and Siebertz explicitly retain the general parameter-dependence gap while obtaining data reductions for restricted digraph classes.

importance.reason: Directed Feedback Vertex Set is a central cycle-deletion problem whose fixed-parameter tractability is established but whose factorial-versus-single-exponential parameter dependence remains unresolved. A single-exponential algorithm or an impossibility theorem would identify a major boundary in parameterized exact algorithms for directed graphs.
importance.basis: Individual review of survey Open Problem 3.3, the SOSA 2025 improvement and the June 2025 primary discussion of the remaining parameter-dependence gap.

sentences: A directed feedback vertex set meets every directed cycle by deleting its vertices.
The question asks for an exact deterministic algorithm with a fixed exponential base in the allowed number of deletions.
The remaining dependence on graph size must be polynomial with an exponent independent of the deletion budget.
Known fixed-parameter algorithms retain a factorial-scale parameter cost, including the checked SOSA 2025 improvement.
This card targets arbitrary digraphs, while the survey’s planar restriction and structural-parameter results remain distinct.

definitions: The input digraph is \(D=([n],E)\), \(n\ge1\), with \(E\subseteq[n]\times[n]\). Self-loops and opposite arcs are allowed; repeated copies of an arc are not represented and have no effect. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices \(v_1,\ldots,v_t\), \(t\ge1\), with arcs \((v_j,v_{j+1})\) for \(j<t\) and \((v_t,v_1)\). Thus self-loops are cycles of length one, and opposite arcs give a cycle of length two. For \(S\subseteq[n]\), the remaining graph is the induced digraph \(D[[n]\setminus S]\). A feedback vertex set is a set \(S\) for which this remaining digraph contains no directed cycle. Its cost is the cardinality \(|S|\); no vertex weights are present. There are no promises of planarity, bounded degree, bounded treewidth, a supplied solution or bounds on cycle length. Use a deterministic multitape Turing machine with one finite program for all \(n,k,D\), no advice and no random bits. A valid input consists of the prefix \(1^n0\), followed by the \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row-major order, followed by exactly \(\ell=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits encoding \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) in most-significant-bit-first binary. The machine must halt and return the correct decision on every valid input. Each Turing-machine transition costs one step, including all input processing and preprocessing. No running-time condition on malformed strings is part of the target. The fixed encoding has length polynomial in \(n\), so ordinary polynomial-time changes of explicit graph encoding only alter the permitted polynomial factor. The quantified constants \(A,c,d\) are independent of \(n,k,D\). The target is worst-case exact decision, including NO instances; it requires neither an optimal deletion set nor enumeration of all solutions.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction of the specified deterministic algorithm with its correctness and \(A2^{ck}(n+1)^d\) worst-case bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm and constants exist. A \(2^{O(k\log k)}n^{O(1)}\) algorithm, an exponent depending on \(k\) in the polynomial input-size factor, an approximation, or a result for restricted graph classes is insufficient for the affirmative answer. A lower bound conditional on an additional unproved hypothesis establishes only that conditional version of the negative statement.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 3.3 groups the general vertex-deletion and arc-deletion questions and separately asks about planar vertex deletion. This card selects the unrestricted vertex-deletion question and makes the deterministic algorithm convention explicit. A positive answer also covers planar digraphs; a negative answer for unrestricted inputs alone would not settle that subclass.

The general unweighted vertex and arc versions have parameter-preserving polynomial reductions between them, so their single-exponential fixed-parameter existence questions are equivalent. Planarity is an additional restriction and is not presumed to be preserved by those general reductions.

The survey records the established \(k^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}\) parameterized running time and asks whether it can become \(2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}\). Both are fixed-parameter bounds, but the exponent \(k\log k\) in the former is not bounded by a constant times \(k\).

Xiong and Xiao’s SOSA 2025 result improves the bound to \(O(k!\,2^{o(k)}(n+m))\), where \(m\) is the number of arcs. The factorial term remains, so this result is not a single-exponential algorithm in the deletion budget.

The June 2025 Acta Informatica paper still calls improving the general \(2^{O(k\log k)}\) dependence to \(2^{o(k\log k)}\) a major open problem. Its positive results exploit additional graph structure, and bounds exponential in a treewidth or cycle-length parameter are not bounds exponential only in the deletion budget.
